comment: The evaluation matrix. Each case is one build; a build is two Opus calls and about
two minutes, so this list is deliberately short and every entry earns its place by
varying an axis the checks actually read.
Axes covered: colour count (1, 2, 4), whether the commander has a tribe, bracket
(casual / default / optimized), and price tier. `tribe` is stated rather than derived
so the density check has something honest to measure against.

Suggestion cases are one call rather than two and cost far less than a build, so the shortlist is cheaper to cover than the deck. They fail differently — wrong colours, a padded list, a reason that gestures instead of explaining — and get their own checks.

cases.why: Mono-colour and tribal: the simplest mana base, so a colour-source failure here is the code's fault, not the commander's.
Go-wide tokens: the archetype §6.4 inverts, so symmetrical mass removal here should be near zero.
The case that exposed the tribe-hint bug. Kept as the regression watch.
No tribe: the deck has to be balanced on roles alone, with no theme to lean on.
Four colours: the hardest mana base, and where §3.2's source counts bite hardest.
Casual floor. No tutors and no Game Changers, against the same commander as the default case.
Optimized ceiling. Game Changers are permitted here and nowhere below, so this pairs with meren-b1 to show the bracket moves anything at all.
The price ceiling, on the commander whose unconstrained build put five cards over $13.
Two colours, exactly. The complaint that started this was picking green and black and being offered a mono-green commander.
A single colour, where a subset rule and an exact-match rule would disagree.
No colour constraint at bracket 4, so the colour check stands down and the Game Changer gate opens.
